second_order: arguing over what makes an April Fools joke worth doing
theme_note: Participants work out whether a one-day joke is funny, fair, timely, or worth the disruption. The codes vary from proposing and defending jokes to criticizing annoyance, low effort, repetition, and personal attacks around that criticism.

second_order: finding a place for a CS:GO mark
theme_note: Participants look for a viable way for r/globaloffensive to appear on Place: asking where its presence is, proposing a representative signature, choosing a candidate picture, and recruiting initial help. The proposals vary from phrases and a 1G mark to the CS emblem, and early replies range from refusal to tentative uptake.

second_order: building out the logo and nearby CS:GO pictures
theme_note: Participants turn selected images into pixels by sharing templates and coordinates, choosing direction and scale, starting outlines, adding letters, weapons, team marks, and nearby symbols, and correcting construction mistakes. What varies is the object and stage of work, from first starts to later extensions around an established logo.
regrouped_from: split from an initial making-a-mark grouping because executing and extending a selected image differs from finding a target and recruiting a start

second_order: trying to fool people with fake CS:GO news and features
theme_note: Participants manufacture and test believable CS:GO news, updates, skins, roster moves, and exploits in order to fool one another. What varies is the prop used, how quickly readers check the date, and whether being fooled produces praise, frustration, or market effects.
regrouped_from: split from an initial local-April-Fools grouping because performing a deception is not the same practice as debating whether a joke is worthwhile

theme_note: Participants orient newcomers to Place by explaining the shared canvas, the per-person cooldown, coordinates, collective takeovers, and template-based coordination. Questions arrive both during construction and after closure, so the detail ranges from placing one pixel to reconstructing the event for latecomers.

second_order: playing CS:GO as if it were Overwatch
theme_note: Participants carry the borrowed Overwatch premise into posts and replies by renaming weapons and plays as heroes, sending ordinary CS:GO questions to the 'wrong' subreddit, and answering in Overwatch character. The performance ranges from brief vocabulary swaps to whole mock gameplay discussions.
regrouped_from: split from an initial Overwatch-swap grouping because acting inside the fiction differs from interpreting the changed subreddit

second_order: figuring out and judging the Overwatch makeover
theme_note: Participants notice, explain, try, praise, reject, and work around the subreddit’s Overwatch-style skin and flair remap. The common practice is handling the changed room itself; variation lies in confusion, aesthetic judgment, moderator attribution, accessibility complaints, and requests to keep or disable features.
regrouped_from: split from an initial Overwatch-swap grouping because handling the room’s design and flairs differs from role-playing Overwatch

second_order: putting on a Bot World Championship
theme_note: Participants stage and promote a Bot World Championship as part of the room’s April Fools play. The small theme ranges from inviting viewers and celebrating a knife fight to proposing follow-up bot showmatches.

second_order: moderating Place links while people mobilize
theme_note: The subreddit’s automated moderation enforces link and participation rules on Place mobilization posts. The same practice interrupts calls to defend, expand, or help other game communities, with variation in the link defect named and whether a direct replacement link is supplied.

second_order: keeping ordinary CS:GO business going through the joke
theme_note: Participants keep an ordinary match discussion and practical help running while the subreddit joke interferes with presentation. The practice includes hand-making a match thread, restoring its usual links and statistics, evaluating play, and explicitly setting the joke aside to help.

second_order: fighting over unwanted edits to the logo
theme_note: Participants fight over what should remain in the shared image: defenders repair stray pixels and genital edits, while other members deliberately add or test those edits. The practice varies between emergency calls, patient repair, joking grief, and post-closure claims about who defended or defaced it.
regrouped_from: split from an initial logo-maintenance grouping because the codes include both deliberate defacement and repair of the same contested image

second_order: using scripts and bots to hold the picture
theme_note: Participants use, distribute, retract, and argue over scripts or bots that place and correct pixels. Variation lies in building versus defending, technical instructions and rate limits, bans, and the ethical dispute between keeping art clean and destroying the point of one-person pixel placement.
regrouped_from: split from an initial logo-maintenance grouping because automated placement brought a distinct technical and ethical practice

second_order: making peace, taking space and trading help
theme_note: Participants negotiate crowded canvas space by attacking, refusing attacks, proposing truces, preserving neighbours, relocating displaced logos, and exchanging help. The relations vary across the Oilers, Warriors, UK, Mexico, TF2, Dota, osu and other neighbours, and the record often preserves only r/globaloffensive’s side.
regrouped_from: split from an initial logo-maintenance grouping because negotiating with neighbours is not the same practice as repairing pixels

second_order: celebrating and judging what the canvas became
theme_note: Participants take stock of the canvas work by celebrating completion, judging the frozen logo, assigning credit, replaying timelapses, and debating what its scars and odd shapes mean. Variation lies between pride in teamwork, disappointment with the finish, individual credit, and retrospective jokes about the battle.

second_order: pushing back on Place taking over the subreddit
theme_note: Participants resist the volume or demands of Place activity by saying the room has already proved itself, refusing reinforcements, asking people to stop posting, suggesting filters, or letting an attack happen. The objections vary between fatigue with posts and refusal to spend effort on another logo.

second_order: turning the finished canvas into a keepsake
theme_note: Participants preserve and reuse the finished canvas after placement closes, chiefly by turning it into a proposed AWP skin and later posting memorial or visual callbacks. The practice ranges from workshop redesign and copyright discussion to thin title-only reminders such as 'Forever Place' and 'Crisp Clean Lock Bois.'
regrouped_from: split from an initial retrospective grouping because adapting the frozen canvas into a skin or memorial object differs from judging the event’s outcome
